sections.h2: Does North Carolina charge a separate tax on profit from a house sale?
sections.html:
No. The Department of Revenue's rate page lists one flat individual rate and no separate rate for gains. Profit from a home sale that stays taxable after federal rules is folded into the same state income calculation as paychecks.

The calculation begins with federal adjusted gross income. G.S. 105-153.5, headed "Modifications to adjusted gross income," then lists what a North Carolina taxpayer may subtract or must add back before reaching state taxable income. The rest of this page walks through the pieces a seller is most likely to meet.

sections.h2: What flat rate applies to a 2026 sale?
sections.html:
NCDOR prints 3.99% for taxable years after 2025 and 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025. It also warns that further rate changes could apply from 2027 on, depending on triggers written into Session Law 2023-134.

sections.h2: When does the IRS let you keep the gain on a main home?
sections.html:
Federal law shelters up to $250,000 of gain from income, or $500,000 on a joint return, for a qualifying main home. Because the state return starts from the federal figure, a sheltered gain generally stays out of North Carolina income too.

Two timing tests apply within the five years that end on the closing date:

  • You owned the house for 24 months or more.
  • You lived in it as your home for 24 months or more.
  • On a joint return, one spouse may meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • A different home whose gain you excluded in the previous two years generally disqualifies this sale.

The months can be split between periods. Military, foreign service and intelligence personnel on qualifying extended duty can stretch the look-back period by up to 10 years. Publication 523 has the full rules.

sections.h2: What must you report, and who has to file in North Carolina?
sections.html:
If the closing agent issues a Form 1099-S, the sale goes on your federal return even when all the gain is excludable, and it goes there whenever part of the gain cannot be excluded. The IRS names Schedule D and Form 8949 for the reporting.

For the state return, NCDOR sets a gross income floor by filing status for tax year 2025:

  • Single: file if federal gross income exceeds $12,750.
  • Head of household: $19,125.
  • Married filing jointly: $25,500.
  • Qualifying surviving spouse: $25,500.

A seller who moved into or out of North Carolina during the year is a part-year resident and files Form D-400 with Schedule PN, which apportions income. If the buyer pays over several years, the installment method applies unless you elect out, and the exclusion remains available.

sections.h2: What if the seller lives outside North Carolina?
sections.html:
A nonresident who sells a North Carolina house owes state income tax on the gain. The NCDOR form NC-1099NRS says gain recognized for federal purposes from real property in the state is also subject to North Carolina income tax, and the seller must file a state return and pay on that portion of federal taxable income.

The buyer has a duty too. The instructions require any buyer of North Carolina real property from a nonresident individual, partnership, estate or trust to file Form NC-1099NRS with the Department of Revenue within 15 days after closing, and to send the seller a copy. The report lists the seller, the property location, the closing date and the gross sales price, including associated tangible personal property.

Estimated tax may also come into play. The form says a nonresident must make estimated payments if they expect to owe $1,000 or more and expect withholding and credits to cover less than 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's. And North Carolina did not conform to the federal deferral for gains invested in a qualified Opportunity Fund, so those gains must be included in a nonresident seller's state tax.

sections.h2: How is a taxable gain taxed federally?
sections.html:
Property held for more than a year produces long-term gain. For tax years beginning in 2025 the IRS puts the rate on most net capital gain at 15% or less for most individuals, while gain on property held a year or less is taxed as ordinary income.

IRS breakpoints for 2025:

  • 0%: taxable income up to $48,350 (single), $96,700 (joint) or $64,750 (head of household).
  • 15%: above those levels, topping out at $533,400 (single), $600,050 (joint) or $566,700 (head of household).
  • 20%: the part of income above the 15% ceiling.
  • 25% maximum: the portion that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property.

High earners may also owe the net investment income tax, and a large gain may call for estimated tax payments. If you sell a personal home at a loss, the IRS says the loss cannot be deducted.

sections.h2: What changes if you inherited the house or rented it out?
sections.html:
Heirs have different basis rules. The IRS says to consult Publication 551 for property received by gift or inheritance, and it notes holding-period exceptions for property acquired from a decedent, covered in Publication 544.

North Carolina no longer has an estate tax, since G.S. 105-32.1 through 105-32.8 were repealed by Session Laws 2013-316 for deaths on or after January 1, 2013. After an estate passes the house on, state tax matters again only when the heir sells and has income to report.

A rental house faces the same two-year use test as any other. The IRS also caps unrecaptured section 1250 gain at 25%, so a landlord should have a CPA run the numbers before a contract is signed.

sections.h2: Which state adjustments touch a home seller's North Carolina return?
sections.html:
G.S. 105-153.5 holds several rules that interact with a sale:

  • Standard deduction: $12,750 for single and married filing separately, $19,125 for head of household, $25,500 for married filing jointly or a surviving spouse.
  • Itemized housing costs: qualified-residence mortgage interest plus real estate taxes together may not exceed $20,000, and spouses share one cap.
  • Other itemized lines: medical and dental expenses, and charitable gifts.
  • Opportunity Fund gains: gain that federal law defers into a qualified fund is added back for state purposes, and a matching deduction follows later so the same income is not taxed twice.
  • Basis gaps: when state basis and federal basis differ, an adjustment is made in the year of the sale.

For 2014 through 2025, the statute also made owners add back mortgage debt forgiven on a principal residence that federal law excluded. A seller who completed a short sale or loan forgiveness in those years should ask a tax professional how that rule applied.

sections.h2: Is the deed excise tax part of this?
sections.html:
No. The excise tax is a transfer charge paid by the seller to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded, set at $1.00 for each $500.00 of value or fraction of it. It never replaces the income tax.

Keep the closing statement anyway. The IRS defines a gain as the amount realized minus adjusted basis, with basis generally meaning what the owner paid, so your preparer needs your purchase papers and improvement receipts as well as the sale documents.

faqs.q: Is there a North Carolina capital gains tax rate for homes?
faqs.a: No separate rate exists. The state taxes the gain through its flat income tax, 3.99% for taxable years after 2025.

faqs.q: How much gain can I exclude on a North Carolina home?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the IRS ownership and use tests for 24 months within the last five years. The two-year limit on repeat use also applies.

faqs.q: Do I report a North Carolina home sale that has no taxable gain?
faqs.a: Yes when you receive a Form 1099-S. The IRS wants the sale reported even if the gain is fully excludable.

faqs.q: What did North Carolina charge in 2025?
faqs.a: NCDOR lists 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025. The rate is 3.99% for the years after.

faqs.q: Does North Carolina tax an inherited house at death?
faqs.a: No estate tax applies for deaths on or after January 1, 2013. An heir who later sells the house may still owe income tax on any gain.
